database.what: Everything PostgreSQL will tell this service about itself, and the state of the schema this service owns in it.
persistence.why.notPostgres: persistence.mode is "{{mode}}", so this service has no database to report on. `memory` writes nothing at all and `ldif` writes RFC 2849 files — neither has a connection, a pool or a catalog. Set persistence.mode to `postgres` (it is restart-only: the store is opened before the listener binds).
persistence.why.noStore: persistence.mode is "postgres" and this process has NO OPEN STORE. That is a fault rather than a configuration: the store is opened from persistence.start() before the listener binds, and a failure there is fatal — so a running service in this state has had its store stopped underneath it. The startup log names what happened.
persistence.why.noMetrics: the open driver reports no metrics function, which means a build of persistence_postgres.js older than 2026-09-11.
postgres.probes.server.what: Which PostgreSQL this is, who this service is connected AS, and how long the server has been up.
postgres.probes.size.what: How much disk this database occupies.
postgres.probes.database.what: Every counter PostgreSQL keeps for this database: commits and rollbacks, blocks read against blocks found in cache, tuples in every direction, deadlocks, temp files, and the I/O and session timings where the server collects them.
postgres.probes.conflicts.what: Queries cancelled by recovery conflicts. All zero on a server that is not a standby, which is the ordinary case here.
postgres.probes.connections.what: How many backends this database has, against the server's limit.
postgres.probes.backends.what: One row per backend on this database. A backend belonging to another role shows as a row with its state and its query withheld, which is what a non-monitoring role is shown.
postgres.probes.locks.what: Locks held and waited for, by mode. A waiting lock on a mock is almost always this service contending with itself across the request-worker pool.
postgres.probes.bgwriter.what: The background writer. ELEVEN columns before PostgreSQL 17 and FOUR from 17, when the checkpoint counters moved out of it — which is why this asks for all of them rather than naming any.
postgres.probes.checkpointer.what: The checkpointer. A view of its own since PostgreSQL 17; before that these counters are the tail of pg_stat_bgwriter above.
postgres.probes.wal.what: Write-ahead log generation. PostgreSQL 14 and later.
postgres.probes.archiver.what: WAL archiving. All zero unless archive_mode is on, which it is not in any stack this repository ships.
postgres.probes.replication.what: Standbys streaming from this server. EMPTY is the ordinary answer, and it is also what a role without pg_monitor is shown when there ARE standbys — so an empty table here is two different facts and the page says which one it cannot tell apart.
postgres.probes.tables.what: Every counter PostgreSQL keeps per table: sequential and index scans, tuples in every direction, live and dead rows, and when each was last vacuumed and analysed.
postgres.probes.tableIo.what: Per-table block I/O: how much came out of the buffer cache and how much off disk, for the heap, its indexes and its TOAST.
postgres.probes.sizes.what: How much disk each table occupies, split into the heap, its indexes and its TOAST, with the planner's row estimate.
postgres.probes.indexes.what: Every index, how often it has been scanned, how big it is, and whether it is a primary key or unique.
postgres.probes.columns.what: Every column of every table this service owns, with its type, whether it may be null, and its default.
postgres.probes.constraints.what: Primary keys, unique constraints, foreign keys and checks.
postgres.probes.settings.what: Every setting an operator has changed from its built-in default, and where it was set — plus the handful that matter whether or not anybody touched them.
